items.title: Nature has spent billions of years fighting bacteria. AI could help us learn its secrets
items.summary: Tiny viruses that infect bacteria could one day help us tackle infections that antibiotics can no longer treat. But first, scientists need to understand how these viruses work, and artificial intelligence could provide them with a powerful way to do that.

items.title: How healthier farm animals can cut greenhouse gas emissions
items.summary: When a dairy cow miscarries, a farmer loses far more than an unborn calf. Feed has been grown, land and water have been used, and greenhouse gases have been released during the cow's pregnancy, but milk production, a future animal and income are lost.

items.title: "Neuroni gladi" imaju neočekivanu ulogu u djelovanju Ozempica, pokazala studija
items.summary: NOVA studija otkriva da Ozempic djeluje i putem "neurona gladi" koji potiču tijelo na aktivnije trošenje masnih zaliha i dugoročno mršavljenje.

items.title: Exploring the moon will require rovers that can think for themselves
items.summary: NASA is planning to send three small rovers to the moon with a single instruction: Work out among yourselves how to explore a patch of ground.

items.title: Topical clove oil for canine sarcoptic mange promises faster, plant-based treatment
items.summary: Canine sarcoptic mange (scabies) is a skin condition in which microscopic mites (Sarcoptes scabiei) infest dogs' skin. items.title: Early-universe plasma may have stopped dark photons from heating cosmos
items.summary: A new paper published in Physical Review Letters reveals that a leading dark matter candidate—the hypothetical "dark photon"—would not have heated the early universe as previously thought. The finding opens a vast region for experimental searches and could change the hunt for dark matter.

items.title: Neptune's tiny moons tell the story of Triton's destructive capture
items.summary: Neptune's moon and ring system stand out among the giant planets because of the strange imbalance between its one very large moon and its many tiny moons. items.title: Scientists detect a surprising shift in human blood as CO2 rises
items.summary: Rising carbon dioxide in the atmosphere may be leaving a measurable imprint inside the human body. Researchers analyzing more than two decades of U.S. health data found that blood bicarbonate levels have climbed about 7% since 1999, while calcium and phosphorus have declined—changes that closely tra

items.title: When gut microbes run low on fiber, they may start eating you
items.summary: Gut microbes need something to eat, and when fiber is limited, they may begin consuming proteins from the mucus lining that protects the gut. Researchers found that fiber can suppress this process, while indigestible plant proteins help microbes produce more beneficial compounds.

items.title: A 30-year-old fossil was hiding bones from a mysterious ancient sea monster
items.summary: Fossils collected in Osaka more than 30 years ago have revealed a surprise hiding in plain sight: four previously unrecognized bones from a giant Cretaceous mosasaur. items.title: Common food preservative linked to rising suicide deaths among young people
items.summary: A widely available food-preservation chemical is emerging as a disturbing factor in rising UK suicide deaths, particularly among younger people and men. Researchers say the scale may be underestimated and are calling for urgent restrictions on access and harmful online information.

items.title: One-off campus programs fall short on preventing sexual violence, review finds
items.summary: A recent National Student Safety Survey found that one in six students attending Australian universities had been sexually harassed and one in 20 had been sexually assaulted since starting university.

items.title: A 60-year-old theory about ants, bees and wasps may be wrong
items.summary: Scientists have long thought an unusual genetic system helped ants, bees, and wasps evolve their extraordinary social colonies. A massive new analysis suggests that genetics alone can’t explain it—and the real secret may lie in other traits unique to these insects.

items.title: Tungsten may suffer more radiation damage in fusion reactors than expected
items.summary: Fusion reactors, devices that generate energy by fusing light atomic nuclei at extremely high temperatures, could contribute to ongoing efforts aimed at producing electricity more sustainably. items.title: Nonrepeating photonic crystal may enable more tunable, reliable semiconductor lasers
items.summary: Over the past two decades, photonic-crystal surface-emitting lasers (PCSELs) have shown promise as a type of advanced semiconductor laser useful in defense- and aerospace-related applications. Typically, these devices are made with photonic crystal patterns that repeat across the area of the device.

items.title: Minnesota iron ore could be key to sustainable and lower cost semiconductor
items.summary: For the first time, researchers at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities have demonstrated that the low-purity iron ore prevalent in Minnesota can be used to create semiconductor-quality iron sulfide, also known as "fool's gold" or pyrite. items.title: Four more belugas arrive at Chicago aquarium from shuttered Canadian theme park
items.summary: Four more belugas have arrived at a Chicago aquarium as part of a plan to move Canada's last remaining captive whales from a shuttered theme park to aquariums in the United States and Spain.

items.title: Shackled men in 2,600-year-old Greek mass graves were likely locals, archaeologists find
items.summary: In 2016, archaeologists working at the Phaleron Burial Ground, part of the ancient Attica region, uncovered an astonishing sight: three mass graves dating to the 7th and 6th centuries BCE containing the skeletons of 79 adult men. Many were bound together with metal shackles.
